paraphrased_candidate_observation: Recognizes numerous Indigenous languages while contrasting them with the centrality of Spanish as official/majority language
Includes a linguistic map listing several languages, including maya, mixteco, zapoteco, tarasco, nahua, otomí and tarahumara
Places speakers of Spanish and Indigenous languages within the same national community
Activity on the languages of Mexico connects lexical loans to Spanish and consultation with family or neighbors
Presents the existence of many Indigenous languages as enriching national linguistic culture
State monographs quantify speakers, languages, bilingualism and territorial distribution
Projects ask students to investigate local linguistic diversity and work with words, poems, songs or riddles
In a speaker community, a project allows an informational note to be produced in the Indigenous language to broaden dissemination
Describes state linguistic diversity and in some cases risk of disappearance
References include origin languages, intercultural education, national languages and linguistic discrimination
